strengths: The architecture is simple and practically motivated. Table 1 reports competitive ImageNet accuracy and A100 latency, including 79.3% at 2.1 ms for GmNet-S3 and 81.5% at 2.9 ms for GmNet-S4.

weaknesses: The central theoretical argument does not establish the claimed mechanism. Multiplication can generate higher-frequency harmonics without improving extraction of useful high-frequency input information. Likewise, smoothness of an activation as a scalar function does not directly determine the spatial spectrum of its composition with learned features. Section 3.2 omits the integrability and boundary assumptions needed for its Fourier-decay statement, and neither argument establishes selective noise suppression or improved learning dynamics.

Architectural novelty is limited relative to existing multiplicative blocks such as StarNet and EfficientMod. The proposed gate x·ReLU6(x) is simply a pointwise activation: zero for negative inputs, x² between 0 and 6, and 6x above 6. Its relationship to squared-ReLU and related activation designs needs explicit positioning and controlled comparisons. Calling this self-reinforcing gating does not establish a distinct mechanism.

The experiments do not isolate spectral modulation as the cause of improved accuracy. Accuracy on Fourier-filtered images measures behavior under distribution shift and can reflect changes in contrast, normalization, and overall model quality. Table 5 changes widths/depths to match resources and does not provide enough configuration detail to disentangle gating from spatial mixing and capacity allocation. Its large gains from DWConv or ordinary ReLU6 also require more careful attribution.

It is also unclear which baseline accuracies were reproduced under the stated training recipe.

Claims of robustness and selective rejection of high-frequency noise remain unsupported. Appendix A.7 reports only an underspecified CIFAR-10 PGD comparison between ReLU and GELU gates, with slightly worse robustness for ReLU. Reproducibility and interpretation remain incomplete: the kernel-bandwidth statistic is not operationally defined, downstream training schedules are missing, and 'five testings' does not clarify independent training runs or uncertainty. strengths: The architecture is simple and reports competitive ImageNet accuracy–GPU latency trade-offs. Table 1 gives GmNet-S3 79.3% accuracy at 2.1 ms and GmNet-S4 81.5% at 2.9 ms, with measurements on both A100 and iPhone 14.

The empirical investigation includes multiple backbones, frequency cutoffs, activation functions, and gating variants. Table 5 reports three-seed statistics, and Appendix A.10 adds feature-spectrum measurements beyond filtered-image classification.
The appendices provide architectural pseudocode, training configurations, and encouraging transfer results on COCO and ADE20K, as well as a reported improvement when adding the gate to ConvNeXt.
weaknesses: The central theoretical explanation is insufficiently established. Frequency-domain convolution permits spectral mixing but does not establish selective amplification of useful high-frequency information, improved learning, or noise rejection. Section 3.2 also omits the integrability and boundary conditions needed for its Fourier-decay argument and does not justify transferring activation-function smoothness directly to spatial feature spectra. Frequencies of the learned input–output function, spatial image frequencies, and activation-domain frequencies require clearer distinction.

Architectural novelty is limited relative to existing multiplicative vision blocks such as StarNet and EfficientMod. The proposed gate x·ReLU6(x) is itself a scalar activation: zero for negative inputs, quadratic between zero and six, and linear above six. The paper does not convincingly establish why this should be understood as a new adaptive selection mechanism, and its projected-gate comparisons substantially increase parameters rather than providing a matched-budget comparison against the closest alternatives.

The experiments demonstrate correlations more convincingly than the claimed causal mechanism. Better classification of frequency-filtered images can reflect distribution-shift behavior and does not establish that high-frequency learning causes the clean-accuracy gains. Table 14 provides useful supporting observations, but activation magnitude, clipping, optimization, and normalization remain confounded. Table 5's baseline also replaces spatial depthwise convolutions with linear layers; restoring 7×7 convolutions alone improves accuracy from 71.5% to 78.1%, complicating attribution of the overall improvement to gating.

Important performance claims contradict the reported results. The introduction claims 81.3% for GmNet-S3, whereas Tables 1–4 report 79.3%. Section 5.1 claims S3 exceeds RepViT-M1.0 by 1.9 points and MobileOne-S4 by 1.7 points; Table 1 instead implies +0.7 and −0.1 points. These discrepancies materially weaken confidence in the headline comparisons.

The broad state-of-the-art and deployment claims exceed the evidence. GPU results are promising, but mobile superiority is not consistent: RepViT-M1.1 achieves 79.4% at 1.2 ms versus S3's 79.3% at 1.3 ms. Latency batch size, precision, runtime settings, warm-up, and measurement variability are unspecified, and the provenance and training comparability of baseline accuracies need clarification.

The claimed ability to retain useful high frequencies while rejecting noise is not adequately tested. Appendix A.7 reports slightly worse PGD robustness for ReLU than GELU, omits attack parameters, and does not evaluate the proposed ReLU6 GmNet. Corruption and controlled frequency-noise experiments are needed to support the stated robustness mechanism.

Several reproducibility gaps remain despite the useful appendix: kernel bandwidth is not operationally defined, downstream training protocols are incomplete, and 'five testings' does not specify independent training runs or uncertainty. Together with the numerical inconsistencies and unresolved theoretical claims, these issues leave the contribution below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: GmNet offers promising practical accuracy–latency trade-offs. Table 1 reports 79.3% ImageNet accuracy at 2.1 ms A100 latency for S3 and 81.5% at 2.9 ms for S4, with measurements on both GPU and iPhone.

The evaluation includes multiple model scales, activation and gating ablations, three-seed component comparisons, and additional detection, segmentation, and ConvNeXt experiments. These provide useful evidence beyond a single classification result.
The architecture is simple, and the frequency-filtered evaluations and intermediate spectral measurements provide an interesting empirical perspective on multiplicative activations.
weaknesses: The central theoretical explanation is insufficiently established. Multiplication can broaden spectral support, but this does not establish selective amplification of useful input frequencies or faster learning of high-frequency information. Section 3.2 applies Fourier decay arguments without the necessary integrability and boundary assumptions and conflates activation smoothness with the spatial spectrum of composed feature maps. The actual operation is x·σ(x), whose smoothness differs from σ itself; for example, x·ReLU(x) is continuously differentiable.

The experiments demonstrate associations rather than the claimed causal mechanism. Accuracy on frequency-filtered inputs measures behavior under an input distribution shift, not directly the frequencies learned by the classification function. Activation changes also affect optimization, scale, and expressivity. Table 14 supplies useful spectral measurements, but its claim that GELU has the lowest ratio at every stage is contradicted by the stage-2 DW-convolution values: GELU is 0.0381 versus ReLU at 0.0024.

Architectural novelty is limited relative to the already cited multiplicative lightweight networks. The proposed gate is a pointwise activation x·ReLU6(x), combined with familiar depthwise and pointwise convolutions. Comparisons against independent-projection gates increase parameters substantially, so they do not isolate the claimed advantage of sharing representations. Parameter-matched comparisons and stronger positioning against squared or polynomial activations are needed.

Headline results conflict materially with the tables. The introduction claims 81.3% for GmNet-S3, whereas Table 1 reports 79.3%. Section 5.1 claims S3 exceeds RepViT-M1.0 by 1.9 points and MobileOne-S4 by 1.7 points; Table 1 instead implies +0.7 and −0.1 points, respectively. These discrepancies weaken confidence in the performance narrative. Mobile results also show trade-offs rather than uniform superiority: RepViT-M1.1 is slightly more accurate and faster than S3.

Important evaluation details remain unspecified, including latency batch size, numerical precision, GPU runtime, timing protocol, and downstream training schedules. Figure 7 does not operationally define kernel bandwidth. Table 5 adjusts widths and depths without reporting the resulting architectures, making attribution difficult; its nominally matched FLOPs also differ. The abstract's code link is blank, and the supplied manuscript alone does not resolve these reproducibility gaps.

Claims of selective noise suppression and robustness exceed the evidence. Appendix A.7 tests ReLU versus GELU on ResNet18, omits essential PGD settings, and reports lower robustness for ReLU; it does not establish robustness of GmNet's ReLU6 gate. Overall, the promising engineering results do not yet outweigh the unresolved explanatory, reporting, and reproducibility weaknesses for a top-tier acceptance.
